source.title: Reinforcement Pre-Training
source.authors: Qing-Xiu Dong; Li Dong; Yao Tang; Tian-Zhu Ye; Yutao Sun; Zhi-Fang Sui; Fu-Ru Wei

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Applies a compute-scaling analysis to a new training regime, reinforcement pre-training, and reports fitted performance curves.
record.gate_note: The paper fits accuracy-versus-compute curves for RPT. It does not report held-out cross-entropy loss, small-run predictions of larger runs, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. Comparisons in Tables 1–3 concern model accuracy or downstream-task performance, not those scaling-law measures.
record.test_reason: Fits a power-law-plus-offset curve (Eq. 5) of next-token prediction accuracy against RL training compute for reinforcement pre-training, a new training regime. This is a result on whether the power-law form carries over (V5). It is weak: one 14B model, six checkpoints from a single run, about one order of magnitude of compute, and accuracy rather than loss.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct in substance. The authors say RPT accuracy improves consistently with training compute and the fitted curves match observations. They present RPT as a promising scaling paradigm and list establishing actual scaling laws for RPT, broader data and more compute as future work.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses RL-based next-token reasoning on a math corpus, evaluates accuracy at training steps for a 14B model, and fits accuracy against compute. It does not reproduce the original held-out-loss scaling measurements or compute-optimal allocation analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted curves are reported separately for easy, medium, and hard validation data; the paper reports high R² for each split.
record.problems: The scaling evidence is limited to one 14B model, a predominantly mathematical corpus, and a held-out validation set of 200 samples. The plotted accuracy values are not tabulated, and the study does not measure held-out loss.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results relevant to the tested scaling-curve version were left out. Tables 1–3 report prediction or downstream-task comparisons rather than scaling-law fits.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining cross-entropy loss versus parameters, tokens or compute. The paper only cites Kaplan/Hoffmann for this as motivation.
No prediction of larger runs from small-run fits. The curves are fitted to all observed points.
No compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Only one model size is trained.
No depth, width or other shape variation.
Loss (rather than accuracy), scaling across model size or data, ranges beyond about one order of magnitude of compute, and other modalities or regimes.
Downstream results (Tables 2–3) compare single models and are not related to scale or loss. The Figure 4 14B-vs-32B comparison is not a scaling fit.
No comparison of fitting choices or functional forms, and no curve bending examined.

record.verdict_notes: The power-law fit is a performance-trend fit within one training run, not a scaling-law study. The fitted exponents and the asymptote P* are not reported. Table 1 and Figure 4 (RPT-14B matching R1-Distill-32B) are method comparisons and are correctly left out as rows.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether fits from small runs predict the loss of much larger runs.
The loss-minimising parameter and token allocations across fixed-compute budgets.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
The paper fits a power law to next-token prediction accuracy, not held-out loss; it tests only RPT, not other modalities or the other listed training regimes.
Predictable downstream-task scaling with model scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocations on setup and fitting choices, and systematic curve bending.

rows.subject: RPT-14B
rows.operation_detail: Fits next-token prediction accuracy as a power-law function of RPT training compute.
rows.measure: Next-token prediction accuracy on the held-out OmniMATH validation split as a function of RL compute.
rows.value: Figure only; R²=0.995. The text says accuracy improves reliably as training compute increases.
rows.note: The plotted accuracy values are not tabulated. This is a fit to accuracy rather than held-out cross-entropy loss.
rows.check: Link and state stand. The 'scaling' is six checkpoints (100–1200 steps) of one run, spanning roughly 1e20–1e21 FLOPs. A 3-parameter fit to six monotone points makes high R² easy. No alternative functional form is compared. Baseline is correctly 'not stated'.

rows.check: Same caveats as r1: single-run checkpoints, about one decade of compute, accuracy not loss, R² the only goodness-of-fit measure.

rows.check: Same caveats as r1. The hard split has the lowest R² (0.989), but this is still high and the text does not call it a worse fit.

relationships.condition: RPT on R1-Distill-Qwen-14B, OmniMATH validation (200 samples), easy/medium/hard entropy splits, accuracy vs RL compute over about one decade
relationships.reason: Accuracy fits A/C^α+P* with R² 0.995/0.997/0.989 (r1–r3). The evidence is weak: single-run checkpoints, accuracy not loss, short compute range.
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy fitted an offset compute power law with R² of 0.995, 0.997 and 0.989 for easy, medium and hard splits, respectively, across single-run checkpoints over about one decade.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
